summary: Inheritable NFSv4 access control entries can be cancelled out by the umask, a mask that limits permissions on new files. This document lets the client send the umask and the create mode separately so the server can decide the correct permissions.

plainLanguage.summary: A folder's rules about who can touch new files are sometimes overruled by a default setting. This lets the server see both and choose well.

questions: why does umask override nfsv4 acl inheritance
what is the nfsv4 mode_umask attribute

subtitle: How NFSv4 lets the server decide when a file creation mask should override inherited permissions.

tldr.problem: On many systems the umask strips permissions from new files, which cancels out the permissions that inheritable NFSv4 ACEs were meant to grant to named users and groups.
tldr.mechanism: A new NFSv4.2 attribute, mode_umask, carries the requested mode and the umask as two separate values, so the server can ignore the umask when the new object inherits ACEs and apply it otherwise.
tldr.outcome: NFSv4 can give the same behavior as local Linux file systems, where the umask is ignored when ACEs are inherited. It is an optional extension that does not change NFSv4.2 itself.

today: RFC 8275 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Umask Defeats Inheritance
sections.content:
On Unix-like systems each process has a file mode creation mask, the umask. It lists the permissions that must be turned off when a new file system object is created.

Many installations put all ordinary users in the same effective group by default. To stop users from granting each other full access, they use a very restrictive default umask. The side effect is that inherited ACL entries (inheritable ACEs) naming specific users and groups are often ignored, which makes inheritable ACEs useless in some common cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A strict default rule about who may touch new files keeps overruling the special permission the folder wanted to hand out.

sections.title: What Local Systems and NFSv4 Do Today
sections.content:
Section 6.4.1.1 of RFC 7530 recommends that servers SHOULD limit permissions granted to named users and groups in the ACL to no more than the permissions granted by the MODE4_RGRP, MODE4_WGRP and MODE4_XGRP bits.

Linux avoids the problem on local file systems by ignoring the umask whenever a newly created file inherits ACEs from its parent. The same approach should work over NFS, but NFSv4 gives the client no way to send the umask of the process opening the file. Clients also cannot atomically check for inheritable permissions and apply the umask only when needed. The server therefore receives an OPEN whose mode attribute already has the umask applied.
sections.plainLanguage: The server only sees the final answer after the strict rule has already been applied, so it cannot tell what you really asked for.

sections.title: The mode_umask Attribute
sections.content:
The fix is a new attribute named mode_umask, with attribute id 81 and data type mode_umask4. It holds two fields: mu_mode, the mode specified at creation, and mu_umask, the umask of the requesting process. Its access is listed as W (write).

Only the nine low-order mode4 bits of mu_umask are defined. A server MUST return NFS4ERR_INVAL if any other bits are set. The attribute is meaningful only for operations that create objects (CREATE and OPEN); for other operations that take fattr4 arguments the server MUST reject it with NFS4ERR_INVAL. The server also MUST return NFS4ERR_INVAL if the client tries to set both mode and mode_umask in the same operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one blended answer, the client now hands over two separate notes: what the person asked for and what the strict default rule says.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use It
sections.content:
When the server supports mode_umask, a client creating a file should use it in place of mode. It sets mu_mode to the unmodified mode provided by the user and mu_umask to the umask of the requesting process.

The server then decides:

  • On a server that supports ACL attributes, if the object inherits any ACEs from its parent directory, mu_mode SHOULD be used and mu_umask ignored.
  • Otherwise mu_umask MUST be used to limit the mode: every bit set in the umask is turned off, so the new object gets mu_mode & ~mu_umask.
sections.plainLanguage: If the folder has special permission to hand out, the server skips the strict rule. If it does not, the strict rule applies like normal.

sections.title: Compatibility With Existing NFSv4.2
sections.content:
This is an extension to minor version 2 of NFSv4 as described in RFC 8178, and it describes a new OPTIONAL feature. NFSv4.2 servers and clients written without knowledge of it keep interoperating with those that know about it, whether or not they support it.

Because RFC 7862 does not define NFSv4.2 as non-extensible, RFC 8178 treats it as an extensible minor version. This RFC extends NFSv4.2 but does not update RFC 7862 or RFC 7863. The new XDR lines are meant to be extracted with a small shell script and merged into the base XDR from RFC 7863.
sections.plainLanguage: It is an optional add-on. Old and new machines can still talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attribute shifts to the server the decision about when to apply the umask. Because the server MUST apply the umask when there are no inheritable permissions, traditional semantics are preserved when no inheritance mechanism is involved. The only relaxation comes when servers follow the recommendation to ignore the umask in the presence of inheritable permissions.

The RFC notes that ignoring the umask when a POSIX default ACL exists is a practice of long standing that has not given rise to security issues, and that the POSIX default ACL mechanism and NFSv4 permission inheritance are equivalent from a security perspective. It requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The strict rule still applies whenever nothing special is being inherited, so nobody gets extra access by accident.
